newsitem.title: UK: Agenda agreed at N.Ireland talks - sources.
newsitem.headline: Agenda agreed at N.Ireland talks - sources.

text.p: Spurred on by resurgent IRA violence, Northern Ireland's key political parties are close to agreeing an agenda for faltering peace talks after four months of wrangling, political sources said on Monday.
They said pro-British Unionist parties and the Irish nationalist SDLP group were inching towards setting the agenda after intensive bilateral negotiations.
Precise details of the agenda were not yet known but it was likely they would be circulated to parties at the talks for consideration on Tuesday, the sources said.

Agreement would give the talks, which are sponsored by the British and Irish governments and chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, their biggest boost since they were launched with fanfare in June this year.

It would also be seen as a commitment by mainstream parties to the negotiating process in the face of the Irish Republican Army's bombing of Britain's Northern Ireland army base at Lisburn one week ago, the sources said.

Progress at the talks would also deepen the isolation of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, which has been excluded from the talks because of the IRA's decision to end a 17-month ceasefire in February, the sources said.
Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams said on Monday that Britain had squandered an opportunity for real peace talks by setting preconditions for his entry to the negotiations.
He accused British Prime Minister John Major of using the talks to try to disarm the IRA by insisting that it surrender weapons during the negotiations to show a commitment to democratic politics.

The talks group nine parties including the Ulster Unionist Party of David Trimble, the main voice of pro-British Protestants, and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) of Nobel peace prize nominee John Hume.
But they have yet to addrress a single issue or discuss any proposals to reconcile pro-British and pro-Irish citizens or propose solutions to a conflict that killed 3,200 in 27 years.
Instead participants have argued about the brief of Mitchell, President Bill Clinton's Ireland adviser, whom some Unionists fear will sympathise with Irish nationalists.
Parties close to Protestant Loyalist militias appealed to the parties at the talks last week to get down to serious talking to assert the primacy of politics over guerrilla war.
The Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) and Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) are taking part in the negotiations because their Loyalist militia allies have stuck to their own two-year truce.

Fears that Loyalist guerrillas might break their truce to avenge the IRA bombing one week ago of Britain's army base at Lisburn have eased after spokesmen said the militia did not want to be sucked back into violence by the IRA.
